context: A talk for new volunteers at Millbrook City Farm

cues.t: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a city farm giving a talk to new volunteers. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook City Farm. My name's Sean, and I manage the farm. Thank you all for giving up your Saturday morning to be here.

Let me start with a little background. People often assume that the farm was set up to protect rare breeds of animal, because we do keep several of them now. But that only began in the nineteen nineties. When the farm opened in nineteen seventy-eight, the idea was much simpler. A group of local parents had realised that most children in this part of the city had never seen a cow or a sheep, and they wanted to give city children the chance to get close to farm animals. That is still the heart of what we do.

Now, some practical points about volunteering. We're very flexible about time. Some of you will come every day, and some of you will come once a month, and both are absolutely fine. You won't need to buy any special clothing either, because we provide overalls and boots for everyone. There is, however, one thing that isn't optional. Before you work with any of the animals, you must attend the half-day safety course. They run every other Tuesday, and there are dates on the board in the office.

People always ask me which job is the most popular. Everyone expects it to be feeding the animals, and that is popular, of course. The farm shop gets plenty of offers too. But in fact, the role that most volunteers ask for is showing school groups around the farm. If you'd like to do that, put your name down early, because there's a waiting list.

There have been a few changes this year that you should know about. Entry to the farm is still free, and I promise you that will never change. The café is still serving the same menu, much to the relief of our regular visitors. What is different is our opening hours. From November to February we now close at three o'clock instead of four, because it's simply too dark to work safely after that.

And finally, one request. If you notice that an animal seems unwell, please don't phone the vet yourself. Tell a member of staff and we'll deal with it. Visitors are allowed to feed the animals, by the way, as long as they use the bags of feed from the shop. But the one thing I really need you to do is to record your volunteer hours online, on our website, every time you come. Our funding depends on showing how many hours volunteers give us, so it really does matter.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Right, let's look at the map so you can find your way around. You'll notice that the entrance is on the west side of the farm, on the left of the map, so as you come in you're facing east, along the main track.
The farm shop is the very first building you come to. As you walk in through the gate, it's immediately on your right. On your left, opposite the shop, there's a small block with the toilets.

Carry on along the track and you'll arrive in the farmyard. The big building on the north side of the farmyard is the barn. The goat shed is right next to the barn, on its western side, so the goats are the first animals most visitors see.

If you go north from the farmyard you'll come to the pond. A lot of people expect the picnic area to be in the orchard, but we don't allow picnics there, because of the wasps in late summer. Instead, the picnic area is on the southern bank of the pond, where there's plenty of shade.

The vegetable garden takes a bit more finding. Go straight through the farmyard and out the other side, keep going east, then turn south. It's right down in the south-east corner of the farm, and that's where a lot of our weekday volunteers work.
And last of all, the beehives. We keep them as far away from visitors as we possibly can, so they're in the north-east corner, beyond the pond. Please don't take school groups up there.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

陷阱：A 的 rare breeds 是「現在」有，但 that only began in the nineteen nineties，不是成立時的目的；C 完全沒提到。題目問 originally 時，要找「最一開始」的時間點。
